cards.title: Checkmate (incl. back-rank)
cards.idea: Attack the enemy king so it has no legal move. A king trapped on its back rank by its own pawns is the classic pattern.

examples.why: Back-rank mate: the king is boxed in by its own pawns; Re8# along the open file ends it.
Same idea with the queen: Qd8# delivers mate on the undefended back rank.
Ladder mate: Rb8# while the rook on a7 covers the 7th rank — the king has no escape square.

cards.title: Hanging piece (free material)
cards.idea: An undefended enemy piece can simply be taken. Always scan for pieces your opponent left unprotected.

examples.why: The knight on a3 is undefended; Rxa3 wins a whole piece for nothing.
The rook on a5 hangs; Rxa5 wins a full rook.

cards.title: Fork (double attack)
cards.idea: One piece attacks two targets at once; the opponent can save only one. Knights and pawns fork especially well.

examples.why: Knight fork: Nf7+ checks the king and attacks the rook on h8 — after the king moves, take the rook.
Same knight fork against king and rook: Nf7 hits g8 (check) and d8 at once.
Pawn fork: e6 attacks the rook on d7 and the knight on f7 simultaneously — one of them falls.

cards.title: Pin (absolute & relative)
cards.idea: A piece can't (or shouldn't) move because a more valuable piece — or the king — sits behind it on the same line.

examples.why: Absolute pin: Bb5 pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8 — the knight is frozen.
Absolute pin on the file: Re1 pins the knight on e5 to the king on e8.
Relative pin: Bc4 pins the knight on d5 — moving it would lose material along the diagonal.

cards.title: Skewer (the reverse pin)
cards.idea: Attack a valuable piece on a line; when it steps aside, capture the less valuable piece behind it. The king is often the front piece.

examples.why: Re1+ skewers the king on e4 to the queen on e8 — the king must move, then Rxe8 wins the queen.
Rh5+ skewers the king on e5 to the queen on a5 along the rank; the king steps off and Rxa5 wins the queen.

cards.title: Discovered attack (incl. discovered check)
cards.idea: Move one piece to unveil an attack from the piece behind it. When the unveiled attack is a check, the moving piece can grab material with tempo.

examples.why: Ne5 steps off the g-file and discovers check from the rook on g1 — a discovered check, and the knight lands actively.
Nc4 unveils the bishop on a1, giving check along the long diagonal to the king on h8 while the knight escapes with tempo.

cards.title: Double check
cards.idea: Two pieces give check at once — one moving, one discovered. The king MUST move; nothing can block or capture both checkers.

examples.why: Nf6+ checks the king on g8 and simultaneously discovers the rook on g1 — double check, so the king is forced to move.
Ng6+ checks the king on h8 and discovers the bishop on a1 along the diagonal — double check; only a king move is legal.
